blocks.text: Important: your child does not need to be with you until the videos begin. First, let's go over what will happen!
blocks.title: Thinking about leaders!

blocks.text: In this study, your child will watch a video about an election for class president. One student becomes class president, but the way they become leader may differ across videos. Children  also learn different things about the student, such as how smart they are. After watching the video, your child will be asked questions about the student who became class president, the election process, whether the leader seems legitimate, and how well they think the student would be able to help the class.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Purpose: We are broadly studying how children think about leaders. People often have to choose leaders and decide who should have the power and authority to make rules or make decisions for others. We are interested in how children think about what it means to be a good leader, including whether leaders are fair, likeable, competent, or trustworthy. We are also interested in how these judgments shape what children think leaders should be allowed to do, including which actions seem specific to someone in charge and which actions seem like things anyone could do. By studying these ideas, we hope to learn more about how children reason about the social world around them.
For parents ONLY: When deciding what to do, your child will make 7 choices in total.

There are no right or wrong answers to the questions we’re asking – we just want to know what your child thinks, so we kindly ask that you let your child respond freely to the questions. For the duration of the study, please sit behind your child or out of your child's eyesight to avoid influencing their answers. However, if your child needs help clicking their answer choices, please help them do so.

video-consent.summary_statement: We are asking your child to join a research study. Observing your child's behavior during this experimental session will help us to understand how children think about the social world. Study procedures include simple activities, like listening to stories, playing games, and watching videos. If you are interested in learning more about the study, please continue reading, or have someone read to you, the rest of this document before you make your decision. Ask study personnel questions about anything you do not understand. Once you understand the study, please follow the instructions on the right-hand side of the screen to complete the consent process.
video-consent.datause: All of your child’s responses will be held confidential, and all data will be stored on a secure, password-protected Yale drive. Only the researchers involved in this study and those responsible for research oversight (such as representatives of the Yale University Human Research Protection Program, Yale Institutional Review Boards, and others) will have access to any information that could identify you that you provide. We will share it with others if you agree to it or when we have to do it because U.S. or State law requires it. For example, we will tell somebody if we learn that you are hurting a child or an older person. When we publish the results of the research or talk about it in conferences, we will not use your child’s name. We will not ask you for any additional permission.
video-consent.use of data by Lookit: The Lookit core team at MIT will also have access to the data collected during this session, in addition to your account data. They use this data to run and improve Lookit, for instance to provide technical support, check how well data collection is working, or see whether Lookit is reaching a diverse group of families. Lookit stores data indefinitely unless you withdraw your recordings at the end of the study.
video-consent.payment: There are no known risks associated with this study. Although this study will not benefit your child personally, we hope it will add to our understanding of how children learn about the world. If your child says that they do not want to continue participating for any reason, you may end the session immediately with no penalty. We cannot and do not guarantee or promise that you will receive any benefits from this study, apart from the satisfaction of participating in cognitive development research. You will, however, receive $5 e-gift card to thank you for your participation.
video-consent.purpose: We are conducting a research study to examine how children learn and think about the social world.
video-consent.procedures: In this study, your child will watch a video about an election for class president. One student becomes class president, but sometimes they win in a fair way and sometimes in an unfair way. After watching the video, children will be asked questions about the student who became class president, the election process, and what the class president should be able to do. These questions are straightforward, and they will be read to your child. These questions do not have a correct answer. Our only purpose is to uncover how children think and learn. We anticipate that your child’s involvement will require less than 30 minutes.
video-consent.publication of results: The results of this study may be presented at scientific meetings or published in scientific journals. We may publish individual responses that cannot identify children, like looking times or sequences of button presses. We never publish children's birthdates or names. Even if you choose to share your recordings, we never publish information that would make it possible to link recordings with your demographic data.
video-consent.data collection and webcam recording: During the session, you and your child will be recorded by your computer's webcam and microphone. These webcam recordings are sent securely to the Lookit platform, and other data like answers you enter in forms are sent to the Qualtrics platform. You can view your past webcam recordings on Lookit at any time. Data are stored securely on Lookit and Qualtrics servers and by researchers, and are only shared as described in this document. However, there is always a small risk that data transmitted over the internet may be intercepted or that the security of stored data may be compromised.
video-consent.research_rights_statement: You are not waiving any legal claims, rights or remedies because of your participation in this research study. If you are not satisfied with how this study is being conducted, or if you have any concerns, complaints, or general questions about the research or your rights as a participant, please contact the Yale Institutional Review Board (IRB) to speak to someone independent of the research team at 203-785-4688. You can also write to the Yale IRB, Yale University, humansubjects@yale.edu.

textBlocks.text: My name is Alina Dau. I am a scientist who studies how children think about leaders.
In this study, you will learn about a student who wants to become class president.
During the study, your webcam will record a video of you. We will watch this video later so we can remember how you answered the questions.

blocks.text: We are studying how children think about leadership, and what makes someone a legitimate or illegitimate leader. In this study, children heard a short illustrated story about two classrooms electing class presidents. In one classroom, a student became class president by winning the vote fairly. In the other classroom, a student became class president by secretly throwing away votes and adding new ones. We are interested in how children think about leaders, including what makes someone a good or fair leader, if the way a person becomes a leader shapes children’s judgments, and what children think a leader should be able to do.

To understand this, we asked children which student they think is really the class president, which student should be able to pick the lunch monitor, which student could help their class with a math problem, which student might take a toy that does not belong to them, and which student they like better. Their answers help us understand how children think about fairness and what it means to be a leader.
If you would like to learn more about this topic, and topics like it, you can visit our website (https://www.socialcogdev.com/).
Your gift card will arrive within 7 days after participation.
If you have any questions, or if you do not receive your gift card, please contact us through Lookit or email our lab's email address (yalekids@gmail.com).
